title: Multiply Without the Multiplication Operator
followUps: What is the time complexity of your solution in terms of the operands' values and their bit lengths? Why does looping over the smaller operand matter?
Walk through how your code handles negative numbers. What would go wrong if you shifted a negative number right until it reached zero in Python, Java or C?
How would you implement integer division (truncating toward zero) with the same restrictions? What changes about overflow at the edges of a 32-bit range?
Real CPUs multiply in a few cycles. How does hardware do it, and where do shift-and-add ideas still show up (big-number libraries, Karatsuba, multiplying by constants in compilers)?
How would you test this exhaustively enough to be confident, given that you can't compare against the * operator in production code?

interviewer.approach: Shift-and-add (Russian peasant / binary long multiplication). Record the sign as (a < 0) XOR (b < 0) and work on magnitudes. Then, while b > 0: if the lowest bit of b is set, add a to the result; shift a left by one and b right by one. O(log min(|a|, |b|)) iterations if the loop runs over the smaller operand's bits, O(1) space. Equivalent: recursion multiply(a, b) = multiply(a, b >> 1) << 1, plus a when b is odd, giving O(log b) depth; or summing a << i for each set bit i of b. Repeated addition (adding a to itself |b| times) is the brute force: correct but O(|b|), which is up to 6.7 x 10^7 additions here and too slow in Python on the hidden tests; ask for something better if the candidate stops there. Strong candidates handle zero and sign up front, choose the smaller operand to drive the loop, avoid shifting negative numbers, use a 64-bit accumulator, and can extend the idea to division by repeated doubling and subtraction.
hints: What's the simplest correct approach, and how many steps does it take for b = 50 million?
Write b in binary. How can you express a × b as a sum of a, 2a, 4a, 8a, ...? Which of those terms do you need?
Doubling a number is a left shift. Look at b one bit at a time, from the lowest.
Deal with the signs separately: work with absolute values and fix the sign at the end.
pitfalls: Repeated addition, which is O(|b|) and times out on large operands.
Shifting a negative b right until it reaches zero: in Python, Java (>>) and C, -1 >> 1 stays -1, so the loop never ends.
Getting the sign wrong when exactly one operand is negative, or when both are.
Accumulating in a 32-bit integer in Java, C, C++ or Go, so products above 2^31 overflow.
Using a disguised multiplication: Math.imul, **, pow, or repeated doubling with *.
Forgetting the zero cases, or looping over the larger operand when the smaller one would take fewer steps.

dimensions.name: Holding the AI to the constraints and checking signs
dimensions.signals: Confirmed that the AI's code really avoids *, /, % and multiplying library calls; that it runs in O(log) rather than repeated addition; that it handles one or both operands negative, zero, and the largest magnitudes; and that the accumulator is 64-bit. Noticed when the AI shifted a negative number right in a loop.

levels.1: Accepted AI code that uses a forbidden operator, loops forever on negatives, or overflows.
levels.2: Caught constraint or sign bugs only through failing tests.
levels.3: Tested signs, zero and large values deliberately and checked the code for forbidden operators before submitting.
levels.4: Gave the AI the constraints and complexity target up front, reviewed the bit loop line by line, and could explain the binary-expansion argument and extend it to division.

watchFor: Using *, Math.imul, ** or pow somewhere in the solution, sometimes hidden in a helper.
Repeated addition presented as the final answer.
A while (b != 0) loop with b >>= 1 on a negative b, which never terminates in Python, Java or C.
An int accumulator in Java, C, C++ or Go instead of long / long long / int64.
Sign logic that's wrong when both operands are negative.
